Mr. W. M. GERMAN (Welland) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 31, to amend the Civil Service Amendment Act of 1919.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, perhaps the best
explanation I can give is to read the short clause of the bill. It is to amend paragraph 1 of section 2 of the Civil Service Amendment Act of 1919-which is the interpretation clause -by adding thereto these words:
rMr. Graham.]
but does not mean or include officers, clerks or employees whose tenure of office or employment is only seasonal or temporary and who are appointed at the beginning of each seasonal period.
Hon. members will see that it does not touch permanent employees. A year ago the Civil Service Commission recommended that a large number of employees should be taken from its jurisdiction. I have no doubt the intention was to include the class which is mentioned in this amendment, and I believe the commission will approve of the bill. It simply specifies the class that shall be removed from the jurisdiction of the commission -men whose employment begins early in the summer but lasts only during the summer, and who are appointed at each seasonal period as temporary employees. If this amendment is accepted I think it will do away very largely, if not altogether, with one of the prime objections to the Civil Service Act. Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

subtopic: PRESS STATEMENT CONCERNING WELLAND, LINCOLN AND HALDIMAND
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as a member of the special committee appointed by this House to which was referred Bill No. 15, an Act to Readjust the Representation of the House of Commons, introduced by the Prime Minister on the 13th instant, I desire to direct the attention of the leader of the government -I am sorry the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) is not here-and of the members of this House, to a statement which appeared in the Ottawa press of to-day, alleged to have been made by a prominent supporter of the government, dealing with the question referred to this committee. The statement is as follows-

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
subtopic: PRESS STATEMENT CONCERNING WELLAND, LINCOLN AND HALDIMAND
speechtext: I ask the hon gentlemen not to read any article from the press, but rather to give the House a synopsis of it.

subtopic: PRESS STATEMENT CONCERNING WELLAND, LINCOLN AND HALDIMAND
speechtext: It is really a synopsis that is given in the press. However, I will not read it. The effect of the statement is that at a meeting of the Welland county Liberals yesterday the member for Welland (Mr. German) stated that Thorold would be added to Lincoln and Wainfleet to Haldimand under the redistribution act. I would like to ask the leader of the government, in view of the fact that the committee to which the bill was referred, has not only not met but has not yet been notified to meet, whether the government have already decided upon a plan of redistribution and have worked out the details which were supposed to have been submitted to the committee.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
subtopic: PRESS STATEMENT CONCERNING WELLAND, LINCOLN AND HALDIMAND
speechtext: I must ask the hon. member not to insist on that question. He is anticipating legislation which has already been referred to a committee of the House.

subtopic: PRESS STATEMENT CONCERNING WELLAND, LINCOLN AND HALDIMAND
speechtext: I would very respectfully suggest, Mr. Speaker, that there is one question which is certainly in order, namely; was the hon. gentleman authorized to make the statement?

subtopic: PRESS STATEMENT CONCERNING WELLAND, LINCOLN AND HALDIMAND
speechtext:
As I am the gentleman referred to, having attended the annual convention of the Liberal Association in the county of Welland yesterday and made the statement, if I have the permission of the House, I will state exactly what I said. I pointed out that the county of Welland had,
by reason of its great prosperity, increased in population to such an extent that it nearly equalled the population of the two adjoining counties of Lincoln and Haldimand; that it was possible in the redistribution of constituencies certain sections of the county of Welland might be removed therefrom and added to the counties <5f Lincoln and Haldimand so as to adjust the representation according to the regular unit of population; and that if such should happen to be the case, the town of Thorold and the township of Wainfleet, adjoining on either side the counties of Lincoln and Haldimand, would be the only municipalities in the county of Welland that could possibly be removed from the county of Welland and added to the counties of Lincoln and Haldimand; that so far as Thorold was concerned I was quite willing that it should go to the county of Lincoln, and that I preferred to retain Wainfleet as an adjunct of the county of Welland.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health

out under another item in the Main Estimates for salaries. In this instance perhaps my hon. friends will not insist upon the details being printed as will be the case with the other departments. The employees are the deputy minister, the assistant deputy minister, supervisor of expenditure, chief clerk and assistant secretary, head clerk, principal clerk, storekeeper, and one librarian; that is all. The total vote for salaries for the next fiscal year is $29,200. That shows a slight reduction as compared with last year, on account of the services of one employee being dispensed with. The draughtsman, who was needed in former years, is no longer required.
What was his salary?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: It was $2,040. The difference between this year's vote and last year's is not so much as the amount I have just mentioned, on account of statutory increases being granted to some of the employees. I shall be glad to give the salaries of the officials I have named. Deputy minister, $6,000; assistant deputy minister, $5,000; supervisor of expenditure, $5,000. These three are receiving the same salary as last year-no increase. The chief clerk and assistant secretary gets $3,480, which includes a statutory increase of $120; head clerk, $2,880; principal clerk, $2,280; storekeeper, $2,400; librarian, $560. The position of senior draughtsman is done away with, as well as the allowance of $600 for private secretary. That is all that is contained in the civil government list of this department. Hon. gentlemen may say that it is a very small list compared with the amount which is paid out in salaries in this department. That is true, but it has been customary ever since the department was constituted to pay only these few officials under the civil government vote.

We desire to stand by the principle which was conceded by the government the other evening, but in this case the item is small and we can carry the details in our heads. I think we can all understand the brief explanation that has been made. The item shows a reduction, and so far as I am concerned I am perfectly willing to let it go through.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I shall be glad to give the
information. When I was in the committee last year, for the same purpose we had seventeen hospitals administered by the department. speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: My hon. friend is quite right in his contention but I would point out that this department is somewhat different to the others. It is one which has been created out of nothing, and which grew info an institution, expending, at one time, as much as $30,000,000. 25 per cent in the number of inhabitants this year, and there is a reduction in the appropriation of one-eighth. The actual

quite satisfied that I am not asking for anything that I do not require. I think it will be obvious to every hon. gentleman that we cannot reduce the cost of administration of our hospitals proportionately to the number of patients. For instance, if a hospital containing fifty patients costs us, say, $100,600 a year, and we reduce the patients to twenty-five, we shall not be able to make a corresponding reduction in our expenses, for, of course, the overheads, such as heating, light, and so on, are the same. I have gone through these figures very carefully with the officials of the department with a view to reducing them to the lowest possible amount, but it will be recognized that we must have money enough for the purpose for which this vote 'is intended, and the purpose is so noble in itself that the department would fail in the discharge of their duties to our sick soldiers if they tried to get along with a lesser appropriation. speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health

Is it the policy of the department to grant a board of examination upon the application of any pensioner, and then that he should be reexamined, or is it customary to periodically examine pensioners in order to determine whether their pension should be increased or decreased?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Where the pensioner has not been declared permanent by the board he is subjected to a periodical examination. The board, of course, use their own judgment in this regard, but it would be fair to say that they examine about every six months in order to determine whether the pension should be maintained at its actual figure, increased or decreased, or discontinued entirely.
Well, is there any degree of disability which an ex-soldier must suffer before he can be declared a pensioner permanently?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: It is not based so much on the degree of disability as on the nature of the disability. The disability may be only 16 per cent but it may be permanent, as the loss of one ear or the loss of one finger. In such a case the pension would be declared permanent, though it may be only 15 or 20 per cent. In other cases a man may suffer from an ulcer which is attributable to war service. If the ulcer is in the leg and prevents him from walking, he may receive 60 per cent disability pension, and he is subjected to a periodical examination, because that ulcer may be healed in six months or a year or two years, as the case may be, so that it is not based so much on the percentage of disability as on the nature of the disability.
In the case of a pensioner who is not satisfied with the decision of the board of examination, is there anybody to whom he can make an appeal?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Last session the parliamentary committee which dealt with pensions and re-establishment made a recommendation that a certain board of appeal should be appointed for the purpose of hearing appeals by men who had been denied treatment. In every case where an ex-soldier is refused treatment by the medical officials of the department, he has an appeal to that board of appeal which is constituted independently of the department. In order to secure the appeal to this board of appeal, the soldier who is refused treatment must supply the department with a certificate from a regular practising physician stating that in his opinion the illness or the disability from which the
Supply-Re-establishment

man suffers can be traced to his service. In this case, and in every similar case, the appeal is being heard by that board of appeal which has been constituted as a consequence of the recommendation of the committee last year, and the decision of that board is final. That, however, applies only to treatment. Let us come to the case of pension. When an ex-service man applies for a pension his application is dealt with first of all by the pension commissioners. I need not explain what kind of a tribunal that board is. It is constituted by the statute, and the statute is known as the Pension Act. The decision as rendered by the Board of Pension Commissioners is final. Neither the minister, nor the Governor in Council, nor any court in Canada, has any authority to reverse, alter or change the decision of the Board of Pension Commissioners in any way whatsoever. During last session the committee was appointed and investigated questions of pensions and reestablishment. A recommendation was made that a board of appeal be constituted, not only for treatment but also for pensions; but in the case of pensions the appeal exists only when the board in Ottawa refused to agree with the recommendation of the pension examiner in the field. One minute ago I think my hon. friend (Mr. Clark) asked me how many medical representatives the department had in the country. I stated that there were 476. If an applicant for pension lived out in the country was examined by one of the examiners, and that examiner recommended 20 per cent disability pension in his case, and ihe board at headquarters refused to grant the 20 per cent but said it should be only 15 per cent, that would constitute a divergence of opinion between the examiner in the field and the central board, and the man may then bring his case before the board of appeal. But in the case where the recommendation of the examiner in Toronto, Winnipeg, Hamilton or Halifax, is supported and agreed to by the Board of Pension Commissioners, there is no appeal. In other words, there is an appeal in every case for a soldier who wants treatment and is denied treatment, and there is a limited appeal in the case of pensions-limited I say-where a divergence of opinion exists between the recommendation of the examiner and the Board of Pension Commissioners. In every case where the two agree, where, for instance, the board in Toronto recommends 20 per cent and the Board of Pension Commissioners agree that it shall be 20 per cent, there is no appeal, even if the man thinks he is entitled to 30 per cent. I hope I have made this clear.

I think the minister has made the matter fairly clear. The case in point that gave rise to my question was one in which the returned man had been granted 100 per cent disability, and had been refused 100 per cent pension on account of a regulation of the Pension Board cutting a pension in two by reason of the pensioner refusing treatment. That was, I think, partially a mental case. The examiner in the field who had examined this case periodically had reported that this man was still 100 per cent disabled and reported that there was no reason why he should not be receiving 100 per cent pension, but the board did not quite agree with that report, stating that, on account of the regulation, the man was not entitled to 100 per cent disability pension, although he had 100 per cent disability. On account of refusing treatment he is still only getting 50 per cent pension.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: This may be an exceptional case where a man refuses treatment when, in the opinion of the medical officers of the department, he would benefit by it. Of course hon. members will realize that if an ex-soldier suffers from a certain disability, and in the opinion of the medical officials he could be cured or highly improved by treatment, and if, treatment being recommended, the man refuses to submit himself to treatment, the board would be justified in a large measure in reducing his pension. That must be the kind of case my hon. friend refers to.

It is, partly. I doubt very much if any of the medical examiners ever hope to improve this man's condition through treatment. I cannot recall any report of that nature in his case, and yet after going to his father's home he has improved somewhat and would prefer to stay there, rather than to take treatment; yet he is only receiving 50 per cent pension.

I wish to draw the attention of the minister and the committee to a phase of the question which I think has not been mentioned this afternoon, namely as regards the appeal board. The minister has stated very clearly the procedure provided for last year by the Pension Committee. A man who wants an appeal as regards his pension must obtain from a medical officer of the department or his medical man, an opinion which differs from that of the board at Ottawa. That is quite correct, because otherwise, the power of appeal would be open to everyone. At least that was the idea in arranging the matter in that way. In actual practice, this has worked out to what I consider a great and gross injustice as regards returned men seeking to make an appeal. I have only a very limited knowledge of the subject; very few cases come particularly to my knowledge; but I know of three in which the men have been most grossly treated by the board at Ottawa. The man secured from the military doctor, a certificate that he was entitled to a pension, and when he brought his case to me I told him that that enabled him to have an appeal from the decision of the board at Ottawa which said that he was not entitled to a pension. I took up his case, and what did I find? I found-not in one, but in three cases, and I have heard of others from other members-that while the local board, the original board, admitted that their doctor had said that the man was entitled to a pension, they got around that and forbade the appeal to the higher board, because, they said: "We gave this local doctor further information, further light on the subject, and he changed his decision." In other -words, they wrote to the local doctor in Vancouver or Toronto, wherever he might be, stating: "You had better send a new form in,"-number 685, I think it is,-"certifying that this man is not entitled to a pension." and in nine cases out of ten the doctor would do that. The board said that they gave them "further light." Yes, they gave them a hint that they had better change their opinion. Sometimes they did and sometimes they did not. If they did not, perhaps they might have difficulty in getting similar employment in the future. At any rate the committee of last year and this House and the government which passed the act never intended it to be worked out in that way, that when the man got a doctor-in one case two military doctors-who certified that he was entitled to a pension, and his right to an appeal in consequence was taken

away from him, because this board at Ottawa wrote and told the doctors, "You had better change your minds." Such a condition is most unfair to the man and is contrary to the spirit of the law passed last year.
There is only one remedy for it, and it will have eventually to come, that every man will be entitled to appeal, not before a board of doctors, who are very excellent men, but not skilled in the weighing of evidence, but before a Supreme Court judge. That is the proper person for anyone who has a grievance of any description to appeal to, for a Supreme Court judge is skilled in law of evidence and knows how to weigh the testimony adduced before him. A doctor may be a very excellent man, a man of the greatest sympathy, but he is not accustomed to accurately weighing evidence. If the appeal from the beginning is to a Supreme Court judge, there will be a series of precedents established which will not increase appeals but rather will tend to reduce them, because it will be known that along certain lines men will be entitled to certain pensions; and it will possess this great advantage, it will ensure justice to these men and prevent the board from whose decision they are appealing practically blocking the right of appeal in the way that I have indicated.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
In that connection, would the minister inform the committee if in case of an appeal relative to medical treatment the appeal board does not act on the' same evidence as that presented to the board below? It seems to me that this is not a reasonable course to follow, because there would be very few cases in which there would be room for reversal, but there must be room for such when the medical practitioner supplies the certificate required.
A man should be given an opportunity of pressing his appeal before the board. Whoever heard of a court of appeal disposing of a case merely upon the evidence that had been given in the court below without hearing an advocate or someone else in support of the appeal? An appeal is almost useless unless the soldier himself is given an opportunity of appearing and pressing his appeal.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Or his representative?

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I do not know whether that would mean a solicitor or advocate. I think it is the desire of the department to get away from that end of it, and I do believe the soldier himself, would be better satisfied if he had an opportunity to appear personally. Of course, if he chooses to have some one appear

Supply-R e-establishment
on his behalf, very well, if he can go to that expense let him do so. I would suggest that when the appeal is taken an opportunity be given to the soldier to appear in person and support his appeal. It would seem to me reasonable too that his expenses in that connection should be allowed.
While I am on my feet I want to say a word in regard to pensions. This is perhaps not directly in point here, but I think it is an opportune time to bring it to the attention of the minister. I have had two instances brought to my attention where pensions have been withdrawn from widows, and they were not even asked regarding the truth of the evidence received by the department. In the two cases I refer to the evidence involved misconduct. Now, Mr. Chairman, I think it is a very, very serious thing indeed when a widow is deprived of her pension without a hearing and on grounds which involve her social position. I protested these two cases, and one of them is still pending. In no case should a pension be set aside without the person affected being given every opportunity to be heard, and that surely is particularly essential when the honour of a woman is involved. I can refer the minister to the cases I have in mind, if necessary, and I have no doubt there are many others. It seems to me that as a general rule where it has been determined that a person is entitled to a pension the decision should not be reversed before the pensioner has been given an opportunity of being heard in some appropriate manner. I earnestly bring these cases to the attention of the minister.
From conversations I have had with soldiers, I find their main objection is that when an appeal is taken they do not know what is going on, they have no chance of presenting their case ,and in the end they are merely told that their appeal is dismissed, without being informed of the reasons which moved the board to reach its decision. None of us would be satisfied to have an appeal before a court dismissed in this way. To a soldier an appeal in the case of treatment is just as important, probably more so than the average appeal to ordinary litigants, and he should be given the same facilities to support his appeal as are accorded in our law courts.

Mr. Chairman, I want to withdraw my objection to the report of the royal commission not having yet been presented to the House. In view of the statements made by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) I would recommend very strongly to the minister that this matter be referred to the royal commission before they make their report. This is the most serious
charge which has been levelled against the Pension Board since its inception, and if it is true I think one-half the facts have not been told. As a member of the pension committee for three years past, I have never felt satisfied with the administration of the Pension Act by the Pension Commissioners, and was one of those instrumental in recommending that a royal commission be appointed last year to investigate the workings of the commission. I would again very strongly recommend that this matter be referred to the royal commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I will deal for a moment with the observations made by my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill). I stated that in the first place an appeal was granted when there was divergence of opinion between the doctor in the field and headquarters. Cases have occurred where the doctor in the field has recommended, say, 10 per cent disability. Upon receipt of his report the medical officers of the Board of Pension Commissioners have opened correspondence with him with a view of coming to an understanding, representing, as my hon. friend has stated, that the examiner in the field might perhaps waive his first opinion as regards disability. In some cases he has changed his views and has come to the conclusion that headquarters officials were right. So no divergence ultimately existed between the two. I was asked as a minister to express an opinion on the possibility of an appeal being carried to the appeal board in such a case. My opinion is recorded officially. I stated that when in the first place the examiner in the field reported to headquarters a percentage of disability, and it was not agreed to by headquarters, and if as a result of correspondence the examiner in the field changed his view, then I was of opinion that the divergence having existed originally there was still a right of appeal, even if the examiner in the field and headquarters ultimately reached the same view. I have in mind one particular case that .was appealed. The decision of the Board of Pension Commissioners was reversed, but the board refused to carry out the decision of the board of appeal, on the ground that they had ultimately come to an agreement with the examiner in the field. I suppose it is a question for the Department of Justice to decide.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
Should there not be further
legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Perhaps it is a case for legislation.

The minister is a physician; does he think that a board in Ottawa
Supply-Re-establishment

is in a better position to decide upon the disability of a man say three hundred miles away than the physician who is in charge of the case?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I do not.

How is it, then, that they can ask the physician to change his opinion? How can they presume to tell what the disability of a pensioner is when they have not seen the case at all? I have had the commissioners practically tell me that they could decide a pensioner's disability just as well as or better than the man who was in the field.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: In some cases the documents on file would be quite sufficient for a proper discussion of the case; it would not be necessary for the patient himself to be observed at headquarters. Medical cases of the same type are frequently characterized by noticeable differences. A typical illness is typhoid, but among a thousand cases of typhoid no two may be exactly the same. In some cases it is possible to come to a decision on the basis of the file only; in other cases it is not.
These files really come from the men in the field or are based upon information received from them. I am speaking particularly of the determination of the amount of disability.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I was coming to that. The hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Boys) argued that when appeal was taken by a man to the appeal board he should be afforded an opportunity to appear before the board in person. Well, in the majority of cases that would be physically impossible; the man might be unable to travel, or he might not wish to come. But there is a provision under which an exservice man who appeals may be represented or may submit his own case before the board of appeal. If his contention is upheld by the board, the department pays the whole cost; if it is not, he meets the cost himself. This is the first experiment that we have made in providing for appeals from the decision of headquarters. It has been operating only a few months; some decisions have been reversed, and others have been sustained. I have not heard any complaint so far in respect of any case appealed, whether the contention made was maintained or whether it was rejected.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
Would the minister care to venture an opinion with respect to my re-

marks concerning the disallowance of pensions without giving the persons affected an opportunity of being heard?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
There is certainly a good deal in what my hon. friend says. If a man is discharged from hospital with say a 50 per cent pension and if treatment is continued so that after six months the pensioner is, by his own admission as well as according to the report of the physician, entirely cured, I imagine that in such a case the Pension Board would be justified in discontinuing the pension without calling upon the person concerned to state his objections. On general grounds, however, it is perhaps only fair, especially in the case of widows of men who fell on the other side or who died here as a consequence of their war service, that no pension should be discontinued without the pensioner being given an opportunity of stating bis or her case, at least by correspondence.
I think the Board of Pension Commissioners would be ready to adopt that procedure. I must point out once more that when hon. members take the attitude that I have some authority in regard to the Board of Pension Commissioners, they are, if I may be permitted to use the word, mistaken. I have no more power than hon. members opposite have; no more influence upon the board than a lawyer would have upon the judges of the Supreme Court if he were arguing a case before them. The Board of Pension Commissioners is an independent tribunal whose decisions are final. Their powers are defined in an act which was unanimously adopted by this parliament. When I suggest to the ' board that a certain widow is entitled to a pension, they may judge the case on its merits and decide differently without my having any recourse whatever. My powers in this regard are limited to the mere reference of particular cases to them and the request that they give to the application their kind attention, applying to it a generous interpretation of the Pension Act. I am, as it were, the attorney representing before the Pension Board a soldier who has presented his case to me; the board, after examining the file and the correspondence and my recommendation, render a decision, and that is the end of it.

Who is responsible for seeing that the Pension Board carry out the Pension Act-for instance, the recommendations made by the Committee on Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment at the last session and adopted by the House?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
The Pension Board is its own interpreter. At the head of the com-

Supply-Re-establishment
mission is an eminent lawyer; I say that without any hesitation. Col. Thompson is an eminent lawyer. I am not responsible for his appointment, but I am free to admit that he is a lawyer of repute. The other two commissioners are medical men. The pension commissioners interpret the Pension Act as they see fit, and they render their decision according to their interpretation, and I have no power, I repeat, to alter their decisions.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: In making the observations I did, it was not for the purpose of criticising the minister at all. I have great confidence in him. I know he is sympathetic so far as the returned men are concerned, and is doing all he can. He has said that he is an attorney, as it were, for the returned man. In that capacity I appeal to him, and I appeal to him also as the responsible minister. If these grievances, and I believe they are grievances, exist and if legislation is necessary to remedy them, the proper person to appeal to is the minister in his capacity as such. I do urge upon him to look into what I have mentioned for it is a very serious state of affairs to have any woman deprived of her pension without being given a chance to be heard at all, even if there were no question of honour involved, and when that is added the situation is accentuated. If the minister wants me to give the cases I can do so. One is pending at the present time. May I also say while I am on my feet that I have confidence in the board. Any matters that I have had to bring to their attention have always received consideration, and in some cases favourable consideration. It is not a criticism of the board or of the minister, but a criticism of the system. I do not think anybody should be deprived of the right without being given the opportunity of being heard.

I should like to hear what is the minister's view with regard to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) to put this matter of appeal in the hands perhaps of district court judges, who could weigh the evidence impartially, hear the parties at the very place where the returned man happens to be located, gather the evidence and perhaps give a decision on appeal which might in some cases, at least, be much more satisfactory.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I have very grave doubts as to the advisability of referring such cases to a district or superior court judge as the case may be. The appreciation of the strength of an application for pension is mainly based on medical evidence. In ninety-nine cases out of a hundred it is a medical case, and to decide upon such a case in any open court,
bearing in mind that the gentleman who sits there as the presiding 'officer is mainly concerned with law, would not, I believe, give as much satisfaction as might on the surface be expected. I repeat, it is almost exclusively a. medical matter, which has to be decided upon by medical experts.
A man dies. He apparently dies of a chest trouble. He has had whilst on service some manifestation of sickness in the chest; he may have had a cough for a few days. He is tieated in a hospital for a chest condition, and he dies. The autopsy is made, and it is found that this man suffers from a disease of the spleen which in medical opinion was the principal and only cause of death. Though this man was treated in hospital with pay and allowance, the Board of Pension Commissioners will say that he did not die of the illness for which he was treated because medical opinion says that the principal cause of his death war a spleen affection which could not have been contracted on service. That is only one instance. There are thousands of different features in medical and surgical cases. The cases vary as much as human faces. Though two men may look alike they are not exactly similar, and it is more difficult in medical science to find twin cases than it is to find two people as much alike as twins in the ordinary course. It is mainly a question for the appreciation of medical men. There are difficulties, there are grievances. Some are founded, some are not. It is exceedingly delicate to pronounce upon them one way or the other. My personal view is that when a doubt exists, however remote it may be, the applicant should be given the benefit of the doubt. That is my view expressed in hundreds of memoranda sent to the Board of Pension Commissioners. But, of course, they are in the last analysis the men to decide, and I am powerless to alter their decision.

After hearing the very able explanation of the minister, I think it is too bad that he himself is not constituted the appellate court because this commission standing there are very apt to view matters purely from the standpoint of the information which they find on their files, without going deeply into the matter. I am very glad that the minister has made the statement that where there is the least semblance of a doubt the applicant should be given the benefit of the doubt. I believe it is not good policy to put into the hands of the Board of Pension Commissioners here at Ottawa the right to have the final say as to whether or not a person shall receive a pension. I believe, if we are going to have responsible government in this

Supply-Re-establishment

country, that the minister should be the appellate court and I think we all will agree that the present minister would make a very excellent appellate court because his heart would sometimes govern, and I believe in most cases it would not be found to be wrong. It is a grievous fact that it has not been found expedient this year to continue the very excellent Committee on Civil Re-establishment that we had last year, chairmanned by a man who worked day and night to get all the facts and endeavoured in every way possible to see that right was meted out to people who deserved the right. I would urge upon the minister to make that committee a permanent committee of this House so far as it is possible to be made permanent. I would also urge upon hifn to take steps to have an appellate court created for giving a final decision in these pension cases, and if you cannot go to a court of judges, let us go to the minister himself, because if you go to him you will find that he will be prepared to deal out right where right is due. It is all very well to say that a board of medical practitioners have decided so and so. Lawyers disagree, and it is often said that we are a crooked bunch. Doctors disagree and they bury their mistakes. It is not fair that any medical man should decide upon the absolute merits or demerits of a matter from the purely medical standpoint; considerations of law and equity, and what is right and just, should also be held in mind. All of us probably have in our constituencies cases where men are receiving pensions who do not deserve them, and other cases where people who deserve pensions but have not been granted them. It is absolutely necessary, in my opinion, that there should be an appellate court in cases where there is good ground for an appeal. I believe also an opportunity should be afforded of presenting such matters before a committee of the House of Commons. The minister could do an act of justice to the country, and to the returned men in particular, by continuing the committee of last year so ably presided over by my hon. friend from St. Lawrence and St, George (Mr. Marler).

I do not find myself m agreement with the last speaker in his suggestion to make the minister a final court of appeal. My position in that regard is taken largely out of consideration for the minister who, I think, would not want any such job as that wished on him. If that were done I think the minister might well pray to be delivered from his friends. I am of opinion that there should be a court of appeal, in certain cases, such as was provided for last
TMr. Martell.]
year. However, I would like to ask the minister what action he means to take with regard to the case he spoke of that was appealed -in which he said officially there was a case to appeal, whereas the Pension Board decided there was none. I do not think the authority of the Pension Board should extend to Jhis matter. I do not think they should have the final say as to whether there should be an appeal or not. I think that is over-stepping the authority which was vested in the pension board; I do not think it was ever intended to vest any such power in them. I am becoming more convinced all the time that the charges levelled at the pension board last year were justified in view of the statement of the minister that they are doing things in an autocratic manner. I think we all respect the fairness and judgment of the minister, and feel convinced that he will not come to a decision lightly in a matter of this kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: In reply to my hon. friend's question I may say that I have given instructions to secure an opinion from the Department of Justice and it will be their duty to decide whether the regulations should be so amended as to permit an appeal where a divergence has existed between headquarters and the examiner in the field in the first place notwithstanding the fact that, as a result of correspondence, headquarters and the local examiner have come to an agreement.

The hon. member for Carleton, N.B., (Mr. Caldwell) seemed to interpret remarks of the minister as declaring that the pension commissioners had given decisions of an autocratic character. I should like to know from the minister himself if that is a correct interpretation of his remarks.

I made that remark in reference to the fact that the board had overridden an appeal although the minister had declared that there should be one. That was what my remarks had reference to and I still stand by that.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I shall not use the term
"autocratic" although perhaps somebody has merited the appellation.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I do not want to use the term in this case, but the facts were as I have related. I had a conversation with the chairman of the board on the subject in question and as a result he holds to his view and I hold to mine. As far as the interpretation and administration of the Pension Act is concerned he is supreme; I am only the minister.

Supply-Re-establishment
Is he autocratic?
Will the minister say if he is in a position to introduce legislation which will deal fairly with the returned soldier at the present time?

In reference to the complaint that the Board of Pension Commissioners are autocratic I suggest that we do not proceed to enact other legislation which would perhaps render them more so. Perhaps the remedy would be found in removing the members of the board, and I am sure I will take great pleasure in making recommendations to the Civil Service Commission.

I have no doubt that the hon. member would be very glad to see reductions carried out and that he would be prepared to do an awful lot of recommending. The trouble is that the recommendations would all come from one camp. I do not interpret the remarks of the minister as some of the hon. members have done. I remember hearing him say this afternoon that so far as he was able to learn charges against the Pension Board were largely without foundation. I think the minister made that statement ; if I am mistaken he will be good enough to correct me.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
As far as the charges of
conspiracy were concerned. What I said was that there had been different charges levelled against the pension board. There were charges of premeditated conspiracy, for example, and at one of the sittings of the commission of inquiry held in Ottawa it was ad' mitted on all sides that such an accusation could not stand. I think the remark was made by the chairman himself that this charge might be discarded and all parties agreed to that. As to other charges that the board have interpreted too rigidly some clauses of the Pension Act no report has been made to me.

I do not profess to have the intimate knowledge of the charges that the minister has. Apparently, however, all charges of bad or ill faith have disappeared. The matter now to be determined is whether the sections of the act have been properly interpreted. It would seem to me to be perfectly easy for my hon. friend to deal with the question of an appeal. My suggestion to the minister would be to simply make a change in the rules and regulations and provide that an appeal should be subject to his consent and not subject to the consent of the board whose decision is to be appealed from,
That is good argument.

During the discussion this afternoon reference has been made on several occasions to the Board of Pension Commissioners. It will be remembered that last year I was chairman of the special committee which investigated this case, and when I presented the report of the committee to the House last June I intended to say something with respect to the Board of Pension Commissioners. But the matter was placed under the purview of the royal commission, and therefore I said nothing at that time. But I did think then, and still think, that it is only fair to say that I was in constant touch with the Board of Pension Commissioners for a period extending over very many weeks during last session, and I found them most assiduous in their duties in every respect and most sympathetic to the returned men. I did not think there was any kind of conspiracy, nor do I think now that there was any conspiracy, but I will explain that just in a moment. This question of conspiracy came up before the royal commission. I have not any idea what the report of the royal commission will be. I have not been in touch with them, except on one occasion only, and that occasion was to submit to that self-same commission a memorandum which my hon. friend from Calgary West (Mr. Shaw) and I agreed on in this House. The royal commission wanted to see exactly what we agreed upon, so that in the second part of the inquiry it might be dealt with. That is all I know about the matter. I do not know what the royal commission will say, or what their judgment will be, but I know that on the argument which took place before the royal commission on the first scope of the inquiry regarding the conspiracy of the Board of Pension Commissioners, those gentlemen making the charges against the commission more or less withdrew them.
Now let us be fair to the pension commissioners. They have an exceedingly difficult task to perform, and at times it is impossible for them to perform that task to please everybody. I know there are dozens of cases of hardship under the act. I have brought cases before the Board of Pension Commissioners, and have begged and prayed them to let them go through, and they have told me on more than one occasion that they would like, if they could, to grant a certain pension, but, Mr. Chairman, the Board of Pension Commissioners is regulated by the act. The act is there; it was passed by this very House and they cannot go outside of it. Now parts of that act may possibly be unfair. Parts of that act may be cold-
Supply-Re-establishment

hearted, but if it is a question of the Board of Pension Commissioners introducing sentimentality, they cannot do it. We in parliament framed the act, and if it is not right, let us amend it in such a way as to give the Board of Pension Commissioners and the government sufficient control to give pensions where they may be due, or to bring in sentimentality or compassionate feeling where compassionate feeling or sentimentality should come into consideration. But I do not think we should direct the blame to the Board of Pension Commisisoners, because for my part -and I say it quite frankly and openly- I have found them most considerate and assiduous in their duties, and I do not believe the charge of conspiracy laid against them was well founded at all. That is my opinion, and I think I should give it to the House at the present time.

I would like to ask whether it is the policy of the government to treat patients in military hospitals, or whether the policy of nursing hospitals will be continued and the soldiers placed in hospitals run by private or municipal authorities.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
A large number of our patients will ultimately resolve themselves into incurable home patients, and gradually, as the hospitals are being closed, and the process of concentration is proceeded with, we will have to come to this last consideration, how best to care for that residue of men who are disabled for life, chronic cases which cannot be cured. It will be for the minister in charge, if it is not myself, to decide what the proper policy should be in this regard. Evidently the government of Canada is not going to continue to operate fourteen, or even ten. different hospitals in Canada for the active treat-* ment of cases. The process is under way with the object of concentrating, in two, three or four different institutions, all the patients who are now distributed over fourteen institutions. Then it will be for the minister in charge and the government to decide what should best be done in the interest of those soldiers and of the country at large. My hon. friend may have some views and other members may have their own views. It is difficult to say beforehand, but evidently we will have to concentrate, and ultimately use some homes for the soldiers who are now almost chronic cases, and also for a large number of soldiers who, growing in age, and being in distressed circumstances, will require the attention of the public or the government of the country.

It would be a mistake to think that, when we are through dealing with the cases that are now actually under treatment, we are through with the problem. I regret to say that the number of applications for treatment is as large this year as last. Men advanced in age, make their appearance with some disability under the name of rheumatism or something else, which, in the opinion of the soldiers themselves, is due to their war service. So that I say that it will be for the department or the government as time goes on to determine what is best to be done.

Am I correct in drawing the conclusion that it is the intention, even though concentration takes place, to keep soldiers together in one institution, and that they will be housed together and not distributed among the municipal institutions?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: That is the first step of course. What will be done after a few years, when only a few institutions remain, will be decided at the time.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. S. BELAND (Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment):

speechtext:
This expenditure has been decreasing very rapidly during the last four years. The peak load was carried in 1920, when we had 26,000 returned men undergoing vocational training. This number has been reduced gradually until it now amounts to only 224. The only men now entitled to vocational training are those who are dis-

charged from hospital after treatment. The committee is doubtless aware that after the 1st February, 1920, no returned man was admitted for vocational training unless he had enlisted as a minor, or unless he had been undergoing treatment in a hospital. The fact that only men who are discharged from hospital or who had enlisted as minors can be admitted for vocational training, accounts for the small number now being vocationally trained.
