speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Hon. members will notice a very substantial reduction in this item amounting to $1,000,000 for the next fiscal year. There has also been a very large saving under this head in the present fiscal year. The item "salaries" covers salaries to administrative, clerical, medical, dental, technical and training staffs, nurses, orderlies, ward maids, workshop instructors, social service workers, and dining, kitchen, laundry, farm and garden employees; in a word, all those not dealt with under the short list of Civil Government, numbering 7 or 8, for whom we voted an item 'this afternoon. The total staff of the department on the 31st December, 1921, was 4,886; on December 31st, 1922, 3,823. I claim, very modestly, of course, credit for this reduction of 1,063.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Pay and Allowances-
Treatment	$3,000,000
Training	 200,000

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: This item, Mr. Chairman, is for pay and allowances to inpatients in our hospitals and also to outpatients. No doubt hon. members are familiar with the rates paid, so I will not take up the time of the committee in giving the details. The amounts, of course, vary according to whether the patient is a single man or has dependents. There is a substantial reduction also in this item, amounting in the case of treatment to $500,000, and in the case of training to $200,000.
I suppose there is no change in the scale of pay and allowances?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: There is no change in the scale.
The reduction is owing to the smaller number of men under treatment?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: That is so.
How much was used of the $3,900,000 voted last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I can give my hon. friend the figures for nine months only. For treatment we spent $2,189,700, and for training pay and allowances $263,000.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Vocational loans, $15,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: It will be apparent'to hon. members that there is also relatively a very large reduction here of $60,000. This is accounted for by the fact that we have fewer vocational students. The regulations provide for a loan of $500 for the acquisition of tools and equipment by the vocationally trained man to carry on his occupation. If I can trust my memory, we have loaned $630,000 to such men. A very large proportion of these loans has been repaid, the amount now outstanding being in round figures $260,000.
What number of men have taken training?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Two hundred and twenty-four.
How many applications have been made for such loans, and how many have been granted?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: In 1922, 94 applications were received and 80 granted. For the two years, 1920 and 1921, 2,369 applications were received, and 1,801 granted.
Can the hon. minister give the committee the reasons for the disapproval of applications?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I am sorry that I cannot supply the information. I presume that if the official at the head of this branch-who, of course, must use his discretion-came to the conclusion that a vocationally trained man was not very much in earnest, his application would not be approved. In this regard I have never received any complaint.
I am not sure that the minister understood my question. I did not mean the number who took vocational training last year, but the total number who have been trained under this system.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Fifty-one thousand have begun vocational training, of whom 41,000 have completed their course.
That is what I wanted.

What was the amount loaned last year?
Sup-ply-Re-establishment

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: For the nine months ending December 31-that is all I have the figures for-the amount loaned was $18,403.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Of the amount outstanding, which the minister stated to be something over $200,000, what amount is overdue?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I am informed that while it is outstanding, it is not overdue. It is being regularly paid.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: None of it is overdue?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Nothing, I am informed.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: If that is so, it is a very creditable showing; I would like to be sure of it. What rate of interest is charged?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: No interest is charged.
May I ask whether every exsoldier who has undergone vocational training is entitled to this loan?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Yes, he has the right to make application for it, subject to the approval of the official in charge of the branch. A few loans have not been approved, for the reasons I attempted to give a moment ago.
Is there any other reason than that stated by the minister, namely, that the deputy minister was not satisfied that the ex-students were really serious?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Not that I know of.
Are there any other reasons which would be allowed by the regulations? Is it entirely in the discretion of the deputy minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: If the vocationally trained man shows a disposition to engage seriously and earnestly in the occupation for which he was trained, the loan is granted. If the responsible official has reason to believe that the man is not in earnest, that he is not really desirous of engaging in the occupation, the loan is not granted.

I am asking this question because I know of the case of a man who was refused vocational training because he was not drawing a pension. Must one be drawing a pension in order to take advantage of this loan?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I did not quite catch my hon. friend's question. I thought he was asking whether every ex-service man who had undergone vocational training was entitled to a loan.
I was asking that.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I gathered from my hon. friend's last remark that he was asking whether every ex-service man was entitled to vocational training.
Not at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Only those who are disabled and who fall within the class of pensioners are entitled to vocational training.

The minister has misunderstood me. Take the case of a man who has pursued a vocational training course and on making application for a loan is told that he cannot get it because he is not now on pension. There are a number of men who have followed vocational courses but who are not now pensioners.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: There is a certain time following the vocational training course within which application for loan must be made. If it is not made within that time, it cannot be considered.
I quite understand that. I wish to know, the policy of the department in this matter. Does the fact that a man is not drawing a pension prevent him from taking advantage of this loan?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: The regulation is very clear; a man who is not drawing a pension cannot be vocationally trained.
He could very well have been vocationally trained and have had his pension cut off.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
The minister will pardon my insistence, but the information he gives me regarding this $200,000 outstanding is so remarkable and so delightful that I would like to be sure of it. It is very creditable indeed if all these men who have secured loans to the extent of the amount mentioned, of which there is $200,000 outstanding, have paid up so well that no part of the amount is overdue. If that is the case I really think the country should know it; I do not believe there is any other class in the community-business men, professional men or otherwise-who could make such a showing. I should be glad if the minister would confirm the information, which he gave with some little hesitation.
Mi'. BELAND: I can only give my hon. friend the information which is supplied to me here. The total amount loaned was $675,856; cash repayments, $207,000; cancelled loans, $73,000; discontinued loans, $161,000.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I think the minister misapprehends my question. I merely wanted

Supply-Re-establishment
to be sure that of the 8200,000 outstanding, none was overdue.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: That is my information.

The minister has stated that a large number of applications for loans were refused on the ground that the applicants could not satisfy the powers that be that -their intentions were honest, to put it plainly, or that they intended to go ahead with the trades for which they had been trained. The minister states also, however, that every one of these loans has been promptly repaid and that there are no amounts overdue. In that event it would appear that complaints which have come to my attention that some of these men have been harshly treated and have not been granted loans where they were necessary, . are well founded, and that in this matter the department has hewn very close to the line. They have not made a loan without being sure of repayment.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
My hon. friend may have
been in receipt of complaints in this regard. I myself have received a good many complaints from returned men in respect to different matters but I do not remember receiving any on this score. If the hon. gentleman has in mind any cases of that kind, I would like to have them submitted to me for consideration.

The minister must admit that part of the correspondence has not come to his hand. It is not reasonable to suppose that two or three thousand applications for loans would be refused without some complaints being made.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: There could not have been that number during the year, because we had only 224 men under training.
The minister says that of the amount loaned, 173,000 was cancelled. Does that mean that some loans were waived?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Yes.
For special reasons, I presume?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Yes.

I would like to ask the minister a question in reference to a returned man whose case I have in mind. This is a man who is getting a pension. He has taken some vocational training but would like to farm. In fact, he has bought a farm. What would the department do in the way of giving that man a loan? He wanted me to see what I could do for him, and I think this is an opportune time for me to bring the matter up.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: So far as this department is concerned, we are granting loans only to those who have been vocationally trained. My hon. friend is referring, I think, to a soldier who desires to settle on the land.
He has taken vocational training, but would rather go on the farm. He has already bought a farm on his own initiative.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: -The soldiers who desire to settle on the land, if they are not trained for farming, must undergo training.
But this man has been trained. He was on the farm before he went to the front.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: If he wants a loan he must apply to the Soldier Settlement Board, which operates under the Minister of the Interior. The conditions under which such a loan is granted are well known. If this man has already undergone vocational training in our department, the only' loan to which he would be entitled would be $500 so far as we are concerned. That would be only for tools and implements to enable him to carry on the vocation for which he was trained.
On what conditions would the money be loaned?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: It is repayable in instalments in five years.
I was asking about cancellation. Under what circumstances was $73,000 cancelled?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: The men were unable to carry out the contract conditions, and the tools were returned.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Interest on War Service Gratuity and Administration Funds, $22,000.
What is the reason for the increase?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: The balances left with the department are constantly increasing. Many of the men who are undergoing treatment do not desire to avail themselves of their pay, and they leave it with the department; their war service gratuity is also turned over to us from the Militia Department. We pay five per cent on that. It is simply a matter of accounting.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Unemployment relief, $500,000.

What amount was
paid during last year under this head?



Su pply-R e-establisli me nt

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: There was quite a large amount spent last year in unemployment relief. First of all, there was an amount of $650,000 which was voted for 1922-23. This amount has been over-expended at the present time, and as was the ease last year a further amount will be asked in the Supplementary Estimates for the present fiscal year to cover that over-expenditure. Last year, that is the year that came to an end on the 31st of March, 1922, an amount of over $2,000,000 was spent in unemployment relief. I am glad to be able to convey the information that we are not spending nearly so much as last year in unemployment relief. Hon. members of the committee may like to know for what class of soldier this relief is provided. It is only used for the relief of distressed ex-service men who are suffering from a disability, and are therefore pensioners, but whose pension is insufficient to support them and their families.
How many individuals benefited last year under that distribution?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: To the 31st December, 1922, the total number of men assisted was 22,941.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Is the reduction in this item due to fewer applications or to a smaller allowance per man? *

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Nothing is paid out in cash* The officials of the department in every unit satisfy themselves through their social service visitors that a family is in need of assistance, and the assistance may be provided in the way of rent, fuel, food or clothing. The maximum amount that is being paid out this year is $67 per family per month.
if this relief is granted only to men suffering from a disability, how does it happen that you are paying less this year than last? Have they died?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Because there are fewer out of employment. That is the only reason I can see.
Do I understand that it is not for men who are totally disabled, but only for the partially disabled and who are working all the time?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: For the partially disabled, also totally disabled, some of them.
The minister has said that only pensioners are eligible under this scheme. What about those who have commuted their pension and are not now pensioners?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: They are also attended to.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Does the relief come as a result of application or as a result of intervention by local committees? If as a result of application, have there been fewer applications in the last nine months?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: It is granted as a result of application. There have been fewer applications than last year by a large number.

I am sorry to see the minister cutting down the vote for this purpose because if any reduction is to be made it certainly should not be in relief for unemployment. There certainly does exist a large amount of unemployment, especially among the returned soldiers. A large number of these men are not one hundred per cent efficient and after a year or two when they return to regular employment their health goes back on them, and under the existing legislation they cannot qualify for aid because the doctor cannot pass them. Therefore they do not receive anything. In the city from which I come the unemployment situation is just about as bad as it was in 1919, and I do not know what the soldiers who are out of work would do if it were not for the municipal authorities. I am sorry that the minister is curtailing this vote because on the occasion of his visit to Toronto he was very active and did a lot of good work there. Undoubtedly the unemployment situation is very acute in Toronto, as well as in some of the other larger centres of population, because many men flock there from all parts of Canada in the hope of getting work. It has been suggested that it is not necessary at this stage to continue to give out doles but in Toronto we have it on the authority of Dr. Hastings, medical health officer, that the situation demands such aid. Conditions are so bad in fact that the municipal authorities in striking the tax rate have to make provision for relief for the unemployed. The state of unemployment is aggravated by the great amount of sickness which prevails, particularly among the families of returned soldiers.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Operating expenses and working capital, $600,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
This item also shows a decrease of $100,000 for the next fiscal year. Last year we appropriated $700,000 for this purpose. These operating expenses are made up as follows: Telephones, telegrams, postage and car fare; transportation and travelling expenses of staff; stationery and office supplies; insurance and storage; light, heat, and power and water rates; maintenance and repairs to furniture and equipment; automobile

Supply-Re-establishment
expenses; freight expenses; advertising and publicity, and other general expenses. The expense incurred in connection with the royal commission on Pensions and Re-establishment will also be paid out of this vote.
The working capital is for financing the treatment and medical examination of Imperial and other foreign former soldiers, also the operation of the Imperial Pension office. The total amount which was expended on 31st December, 1922, was $486,187.
What is the estimate for the expenses of the royal commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: The sum of $35,000 has been placed in the estimates for that purpose.
Is there any other appropriation elsewhere for that purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: No.
How much was received for the treatment of these patients from other countries last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: This vote is, to a large extent, carrying itself, because the money that is being advanced for the examination and treatment of former Imperial soldiers is being collected from the Imperial government; but the committee will realize, of course, that we have first to make the disbursement and then collect the money from the Imperial authorities. In answer to my hon. friend from Kingston I may say that on the 31st December, 1922, we had received $404,000 for financing the treatment and medical examination of Imperial and other former foreign soldiers. These accounts are not settled until six or seven months after the expenses have been incurred.
I was under the impression that the amount received was something like $600,000. I would ask what becomes of this money?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I am referring only to the
nine months which ended on 31st December, 1922, and, as I have already said, the receipts on that account were $404,000.
Have we a similar arrangement with other countries, for example, with the United States, and under what head shall we find the moneys expended for that purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: We also have an arrangement with the United States for the same purpose. They undertake to care for our soldiers, giving them treatment and so on, and their expenditure is refunded by this department. The arrangement is a reciprocal one.
While we are on that subject, can the minister tell us how many of our returned men are now in the United States? The minister has no idea as to the number?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
There are quite a number but I am unable to give my hon. friend the
exact figures offhand.

I wonder if the minister has looked at all into the question of the large number of ex-service men who have been leaving this country and going to the United States? Has that been drawn to his attention?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I did not know that a very large number of soldiers had left this country, and I would be sorry to learn that such was the case. However, I have no information on the subject.
My hon. friend could not tell us how many pension cheques go to Canadians who are now living in the States?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I will be able to give the information when the item for pensions is under consideration. That is an entirely different item from the one we are now considering.

The hon. member for Kingston put a question as to what became of the moneys collected. I assume they are paid in the ordinary way to the account of the Receiver General and do not go to the minister's department at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: The money goes to the account of the Receiver General.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Employers' Liability Compensation, 175,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
We have spent very little
in this connection. The total expenditure for the ten months ended January 31, 1923, was $14,816. A large amount is being asked this year although not so large as last year. We think that the employers have not been made aware of the provisions that we made to offset the liability for which the employment of the disabled would make them responsible. The regulations provide that any employer of a disabled man whose disability is over 20 per cent may be refunded any money that he would have to pay in rates of assessment or as compensation on account of employing a disabled man. I think that is a very wise provision. It will help to a very large extent tnc disabled men who are otherwise precluded from readily finding employment, on account cf the employers being very diffident in regard
Supply-Re-establishment

to using their service^ for fear of accidents. We are providing this amount, but we have nh idea whatever what amount may be spent It may be $25,000, $50,000, $75,000 or perhaps $100,000. The first consideration we gave to this item led us to ask $175,000, but finding that we spent so little last year, I surmised that perhaps $75,000 would meet the requirements.

I do not think
the vote started at $175,000. I do not think the policy the hon. member is alluding to is his own creation at all. I have a recollection that we started that some time ago. My recollection is that we had a vote of $100,000 in the year 1921 for the same purpose. I do not think we started at $175,000, nor did the idea start with the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
No, I did not say that.
I said that last year I asked for $125,000, of which only $14,000 was expended. I was not referring at all to the former administration. This vote was placed in the estimates last year pursuant to an order in council that had been passed covering any liabilities that an employer might suffer by reason of employing a disabled man in his shop.

The vote was
put in just the same as any other vote in connection with service already being performed. I forget the exact year in which the policy was inaugurated. I entirely agree with the minister that it is a very good thing. He is generally right when he follows the system adopted by the late government. I should like to know what is being done now with a view to letting the manufacturers know just exactly what the situation is. It is something on which we want to spend money rather than save it, because it means we are getting employment for the returned soldier through this means.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I think that it is now pretty generally known amongst the employers, but the department is taking steps to make this provision known to every employer in the country.
What provision is being made to check up the returned men who are reported by the employers as coming under this clause?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
We have one unit in every province, and the officials in the department in every province are in a position to know exactly what the situation is in connection with all manufacturers who make a claim for a refund from the department on account of these disability cases where the men meet
[Mr. Beland.l
with accidents, or on account of special assessment rates to which the manufacturer may be subject. That is as easy a matter to supervise, I should say, as the unemployment relief, for instance, in every large city. I hope this answers my hon. friend's inquiries.

This is a very good form of insurance, but there seems to be some doubt as to whether it is well known in the country. It was only in force a very short time last. year. Would the minister tell the committee how an employee would make an application of this kind and to whom he would apply? Of course, there are some employers of labour who are patriotic enough to employ these men tlifemselves, but there are some cases where they are not willing to take a man with a disability of 20 per cent. I should like the minister to tell us how they can make these applications. I may say I never heard of any complaint. This is a very reliable form of insurance. Many men suffer more than 20 per cent disability. If a man has not 100 per cent efficiency, he has to take a lower rank in the service, and I would like to ascertain whether this desirable form of insurance is generally known.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: There is no need of a special application on the part of the employer. Nobody is excused for ignorance of the law. In this case it is not a statute but an order in council. This order in council has been made known pretty wel 1/ all over the country by this time. Any employer who employs a disabled man with a disability of over 20 per cent, and on that account becomes liable for compensation and also for a special assessment rate, has a right to come to the department for a refund. He need not ma^e any application. _
Will this sum be sufficient to cover the whole of Canada for one year?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Yes, because however reluctant the employers may be to take in their service disabled soldiers, the experience shows that men with disability of 30, 35 or 40 per cent will not meet with accidents much oftener than the other employees. It may be, as my hon. friend suggests, that the amount is too small. I have no possible means of gauging what amount would be required in this instance. It may be $100,000 or it may be only $30,000. It is purely speculative, because it is based on the accidents with which the disabled employees may meet. *

Supply-R e-establish men t
The government stands behind the order in council anyway?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Yes.
And the government are now providing themselves with this amount of money?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Yes.
I think it goes further than my hon. friend pointed out. Not only are we responsible in the case of accidents, but we also pay the, increased premiums to the insurance companies.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Yes, certainly.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Sheltered employment, after care, transportation of the blind, burial expenses of the destitute, etc., $375,000.
Why the increase of 3135,000?

Could the minister let the
committee know if the recommendations of the special parliamentary committee as regards the blind have been carried out? I understood from the minister last session that he was to make a further inquiry regarding the compensation to be paid to these men. Six hundred dollars a year is not very much for a man who has lost his sight, especially, in the larger cities, when he has to pay an attendant to conduct him to any work that he has to do. Many of these blind men, now that the war is over, are receiving very little work and still less sympathy. I think the sum recommended by the organization representing the blind was two or three hundred dollars, but they did not get the money. There is another appropriation

I do not think it is this item-of $10,000 which the House passed unanimously last year for the Canadian Institute for the Blind, which do nearly all the work in Canada for the blind soldiers; but they did not get the money; it was held up in the Finance department. This may not come under this item; but something should be done, especially in the larger cities throughout the country, where the blind have to have guides to lead them around the streets. That was the only thing for which the blind asked last year, and which they did not get. I should like to see them get the increase, I think it is about three or four dollars a week.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
All the recommendations
of the parliamentary committee of last year have been carried out. We have adopted a regulation to provide for an escort in the case
of a totally blind man, and also to defray his transportation expenses if, of course, he does not make a play of travelling all the time. I know my hon. friend has taken a special interest in that particular class of returned soldiers, and the country at large, I am sure, shares his views in that regard. The blind are receiving special treatment at the hands of this parliament, and the recommendations that have been made particularly in their behalf have been carried out. Perhaps I might go a little further and give the committee just a few figures in that connection. Hon gentlemen may be interested to know the number of ex-service men afflicted by total or partial blindness. The total number on record is 2,285, of whom 1,258 are afflicted with blindness on account of loss of one or both eyes, and 1,027 suffer from defective vision, both eyes being' retained. Of this number, 158 are in receipt of a 100 per cent pension. It will be interesting, undoubtedly, for the committee to know that 171 of those having defective eyesight have been fully trained. I will bear in mind what my hon. friend (Mr. Church) says on behalf of the blind. I am sure there is no class of war-disabled men that appeals more strongly to hon. ijjembers and to myself.

There is and has been for some years in the Estimates another appropriation of $10,000 to which my hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Church) has referred. It is number 321, and I see it is put in as a grant to the Canadian National Institute for the Blind under agreement with the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, authorized by order in council of April 2, 1919. It comes by agreement under the minister's department. My hon. friend from Toronto intimated that for some reason or another this $10,000 had not been paid last year. Perhaps the minister can give us some information in regard to that.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
The Auditor General ruled that this amount under the head of Miscellaneous should be paid over to the department for the discharge of their obligations to the National Institute for the Blind. The amount was paid over to our department, and in turn was paid over to the Institute for the Blind. I may say, however, that some of the representatives of that worthy institute came in a delegation to interview the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) and myself. They claim that they are entitled to $10,000 as a grant, besides the $10,000 which they should receive under the agreement with the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment.
Supply-Re-establishment

The representations that they have made to the Minister of Finance and myself have all but convinced us that their contention is probably right. The matter is now under consideration, and it is likely that in the Supplementary Estimates $10,000 further will be provided as the institute, claims.

Can my hon. friend not say that he is already persuaded and tell us that the money will be given? There is no question about the urgency of this matter or the character of the work that is being done by the institute. I am quite sure my hon. friend agrees. Perhaps, he could make this appropriation just large enough to look after the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I do not want to promise, but I make it a policy of always giving more than I promise.
How much of this vote is to go to sheltered employment, how much to after care, how much to transportation of the blind and how much to burial expenses of destitutes?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: For sheltered employment, operation of vetcraft shops and payment of Red Cross societies and similar enterprises, the amount is $320,000; for special tubercular clinics, $15,000; for transportation of the blind, $5,000; and for burial expenses of destitute former soldiers, $10,000.
Does that include the appropriation for the last post fund?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Yes, burial expenses of destitute former soldiers and payment to last post fund.
How much was paid to shops operated by'the Red Cross Society?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
The sheltered employment, through the Red Cross, is just getting under way. We have concluded some arrangements with the Red Cross societies in Winnipeg, Vancouver and Victoria. So far as St. John and Halifax are concerned, it is only a week ago that a deputation from those cities interviewed me on this very subject, and we have made arrangements with them to open vet-craft shops. In the case of Toronto, for reasons that are unknown to me, the department has been unable to come to a definite agreement with the provincial Red Cross society. The department has therefore taken steps to open a vetcraft shop in that city to replace the shop destroyed last winter. We have secured commodious premises for. the purpose on Dundas street, and during my stay in Toronto it was my privilege to inspect them.
fMr. Boland.]
Sheltered employment is one feature of our work in which the minister as well as the officials of the department are keenly interested, for we realize that in this way we can render real service to men who on account of some disability are precluded from entering the open labour market. We have spent little so far in that direction, and the amount which is now being asked is large comparatively, but as far as I am concerned I hope we will spend it all-of course, in a manner to secure the best results. I wish to see established in every large city in Canada a vetcraft shop where problem cases can be employed during a certain number of hours each day at liberal rates of remuneration, for this is not entirely a philanthropic enterprise; it is somewhat of an economic undertaking.
The agreement which we have made with the Red Cross society will, I think, commend itself to every hon. member. It provides that the government shall pay 85 per cent of all capital expenditure and the provincial division of the Red Cross 15 per cent, the equity in the equipment and buildings to remain in both parties in proportion to the percentage of expenditure contributed by each.
These vetcraft shops will be under the direction of a committee of three members appointed by the Red Cross Society. This committee will have control of the type of occupation, the rate of remuneration, the puri hare of supplies, the disposal of the product, the framing of disciplinary measures, and the admission of men to the shops. The Department of Soldier's Civil Re-establishment may appoint two members of its staff to act in an advisory capacity, but the final control in this instance rentains with the Red Cross Society. A board of admission, composed of three doctors, two appointed by the department and one by the society, is to be established in connection with each workshop. This board is to decide what cases shall be admitted to the shop, the nature of the work assigned to each man, the hours of employment, and the termination of the employment on medical grounds. It will be readily recognized that this is absolutely indispensable in dealing with men suffering from disability, or who may be threatened with a recurrence of disability, and who being paid by the hour might be tempted to work longer than would be good for their health.
V'hile we regard this as an economic undertaking, we do not expect that it will be selfsupporting. It would be very satisfactoiy if it were, but I think it is too much to expect this. At all events the department, in view of the representations made to it by the Red

Svpply-Re-establishment
Cross society, has agreed to make good any *deficit to the extent of 75 per cent, it being always understood that no more than $25 per man per month will be contributed by the department.
As I said a short time ago, such an agreement has been arrived at with the provincial Red Cross society in some of the provinces. In others, it has been impossible so far to induce the provincial branch to accept the proposition. We are not at' all deterred by this failure, and are determined to provide employment for this class of disabled men. We have succeeded in establishing a vetcraft shop in Toronto, and it may be that in the course of a few months we will pass it over to the provincial Red Cross branch.
It seemed to me desirable to furnish this information to the committee, because it relates to a somewhat new feature of the work of the department-work which I think is becoming more necessary as the years go by.
Will the minister state what portion of this fund has been earmarked for particular vetcraft shops operated by the Red Cross society?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: A sum of $320,000.

I know. But taking, for
instance, the vetcraft shops established in Toronto and Vancouver, how much will be paid to.each of those shops?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Not until operations have
been carried on for a number of months shall I be in a position to give that information. Of course, on how favourably we can dispose of the product of those shops, will depend the economic outcome of the work. The amount is in a bulk sum because we have concluded agreements only with three branches )f the provincial Red Cross, and in all the other instances, with the exception of St. John and Halifax, we are carrying on the work ourselves on a more or less limited scale. But the intention is to extend these vetcraft shops and so provide more and more employment for this class of disabled soldiers, in the expectation that if the shops are not self-supporting, at least there will be relatively only a small deficit to be met by the department.

Do these vetcraft shops
explain the increase of $135,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
That is the explanation.
The increase is for the purpose of providing sheltered employment to the extremely disabled.
Are any other steps being taken by the government to secure employment for the very large number of disabled soldiers who are at present untrained and unemployed?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: We have in every unit a section known as the unemployment and relief section. When a disabled returned man applies for relief because he lacks employment it is the duty of the officials of that unit to seek employment for him. Last year we provided employment for 18,000 of these applicants throughout Canada.

I am aware of that. But the metho^ is unsatisfactory, because some of these men are not able to compete in the open labour market; even though they secure employment they cannot retain it for any considerable length of time. I had hoped that under this item the government would aim to secure some permanent employment or training for the whole body of returned soldiers who are disabled and unable to compete in the open labour market.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I assure my hon. friend that we are exerting every effort to secure employment for those who are disabled. In 1922 we had 35,000 applications for employment. We placed 18,000 of these; 13,000 applications were withdrawn, and there is a pending placement balance of 4,504. We are endeavouring to secure employment for these in our shop. We do not want to venture upon this vetcraft employment on too large a scale, but if it proves satisfactory we will extend it so that in a year or so we shall be in a position to procure employment for disabled men who cannot find it elsewhere.
How many disabled men are there who are unemployed?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I have no exact date.

The least the country could do for the returned soldier who dies destitute is to provide him with a decent burial. The officers of the department should be instructed to see to it that in a case of that kind the necessary arrangements should be made-whether the funeral is to be a military one, whether there is to be a band or not, and so on. The other day a soldier who had been under treatment in a hospital in Toronto was transferred to London and died there. The body was kept in a morgue or undertakers, I believe, or in a box of some kind, for four weeks; nobody seemed to do anything about providing a decent burial. Friends in Toronto took the matter up with the municipal officials, but nothing could be done. The military authorities were appealed to, but they said he did not come under the last post fund,
Supply-Re-establishment

or in some way did not come under the regulations of the department provided . in such cases, so that nothing could be done. It was proposed to make a house to house canvass to get the money with which to bury him. The city authorities finally said they would look after the matter, and after a good deal of correspondence the burial took place. I hope that the D. S. C. R. officers throughout Canada will receive instructions so that there will be no doubt about how to proceed in matters of this kind, and so that a few paltry dollars will not stand in the way of a destitute soldier being given a decent burial. There should be no conflict between the military authorities, the municipal authorities and the D. S. C. R. in the matter of burying a man who served over four years in France, who had been out of work, and who had a wife and four very small children.
Does the liability compensation apply to men who may be engaged in work in the sheltered employments?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: No.

Will there not be some difficulties arising in that connection? I take it that accidents can occur in connection with the sheltered employments under the Red Cross just as they can in other workshops. Will provision not be made for compensation in the case of accident, as is done under the compensation provisions of the different provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: My hon. friend's suggestion may be well thought out, but the vetcraft shops are being operated by the Red Cross society under an agreement. If claims such as my hon. friend refers to should be presented to the department, I suppose they would be open for consideration.

I have no doubt that the minister has given great care to the preparation of this item and that he has been interested, as many members of the House have been, in the vetcraft shops. But he has not given us any information as to the approximate loss involved in the operation of similar shops which have been in existence for a number of years, and I would like to have that information. I would also ask whether the minister has made any special provision since taking office for the care of neurological patients, which constitute, after all, our most serious problem so far as the returned men are concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
The vetcrafts to which I have referred have been in operation only a few weeks.
I Mr. Church.]
There were some operated two or three years ago, one notably in Hamilton.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: None of these shops was self-supporting.
To what extent were they not?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I have not that information at hand. This afternoon I gave some information with regard to the cases in our mental institutions. The number has very largely increased, whereas the number of cases in other hospitals for general treatment has decreased. These neurological cases are being treated mainly in two hospitals, one at Ste. Anne and the other at Westminster, Ontario.

Unfortunately I was not able to be here this afternoon; if the information is on Hansard, I will not ask the minister to give it a second time. I should be quite willing to accept the figures given with regard to these hospitals; I have no doubt that the neurological cases are being well looked after by the department. There is a class of cases that has come before the committee quite frequently in previous years, and that is the man who is not necessarily ill in the hospital but has a recurrent disability of this nature. What has been done to take care of that class? They are the most difficult cases for the minister and the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
The regulations in this
connection are very elastic. We are far, I think, from being severe when it comes to granting treatment, especially in nervous and mental cases. It will occur to every hon. gentleman how difficult it is some years after a man is discharged to attribute a mental disability to war service, but in every instance we give the man the benefit of the doubt, and that accounts for the number of mental case* in our mental institutions.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Medical advisory and appeal boards, 150,000.

Is the minister contemplating any change of policy with regard to the Christie street hospital, Toronto? This hospital is serving a most useful purpose. I hope there will be no change in policy, and that the government will see its way clear to keeping it open for another year at least.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I can assure my hon.
friend that we have no intention, at the piesent time at least, of discontinuing the Christie street hospital; on the contrary, it is for the time being the policy of the department not only to keep it open but even to concca-

Supply-Health
trate there patients from other institutions. This has been done because there were a large number of vacant beds at the Christie street hospital.

I have had a case referred to me which I would like to look into and bring before the minister. It refers to the Medical Advisory Board, and I would ask the minister if he would be good enough to allow this item to stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Of course I do not want to refuse any reasonble request of my hon. friend, but so far as the Medical Advisory Board is concerned, we discussed it lengthily this afternoon. A number of hon. members have shared in the discussion and a good deal of light has been thrown upon the subject. As a matter of fact, the subject has been almost exhausted. I may say that no money has bten spent so far under this item. It is a revote. The Medical Advisory Board has been sitting for a little time, but no bill of expenditure has yet been furnished.
If I shall have an opportunity of bringing up the case on the Supplementary Estimates, it will be quite sr tisfactory.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Yes, certainly.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. member for Fort William, the former Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment (Mr. Manion) is not here, and will probably want to speak. The minister has passed about $12,000,000 since 3.30 this afternoon, and it seems to me it would not be amiss if he consented to the request of the hon. member for Kingston and let this matter stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I have no intention of refusing the request, but perhaps I might suggest this: There is an item of $32,000,000 for pensions to come up, and I can assure my hon. friend that he will have ample opportunity of discussing any feature of the work of this department on that item.
What steps have been taken to advise the returned men that they have access to this appeal board?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
No special steps have been
taken so far because no publicity expenditure has been incurred. The intention was to await the report of the royal commission on Pensions and Re-establishment so that all the information could be supplied in pamphlet form. I may say to my hon. friend that whenever a case comes before the department where it has been found necessary to refuse an application, the man is notified that if he so desires he may appeal, and the proper
machinery and the procedure is set out for him. I know that in numberless instances in the last three or four months I have written back to applicants setting out what the procedure would be if they desired to appeal.

Under section 4 of the report of the special committee appointed last session on soldiers' re-establishment, there was a recommendation in regard to publicity of this board of appeal. Just what steps have been taken in regard to following out this recommendation of this special parliamentary committee?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I have just explained to
my hon. friend that we were awaiting the report of the royal commission before all that information was conveyed to the veterans. The report is not in yet, but as soon as it comes in we will undertake to supply in pamphlet form, I suppose to every pensioner, . and every returned man, if it is possible, the necessary information. If the report is going to be much delayed, we shall take some means of diffusing the information through some of the veterans' newspapers.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Item agreed to.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: The administration of the Act respecting Food and Drugs, Honey and Maple products, and Opium and Narcotic Drugs, $90,800.

Will the minister give us a little information on this vote. I have a few questions I want to ask having reference to the administration of the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act. Is it the intention of the minister to bring down an amendment correcting an error that occurred in an amendment to the act last year which makes it exceedingly difficult to secure convictions under this act? I think the minister will recall some communications I had with the department, I think with the minister himself, during the year regarding it. For the moment I think the section in question was in number 21. I submitted to him the opinion of one of the chiefs of police and it was pointed out, I know, in the reply that there had been an oversight, or that something had been left out, in draughting the amendment in question.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
At the present time I do not recollect what the particular point was that my hon. friend brought to my attention but I may inform him that it is my intention to submit to the House, a little later in the session, a consolidation of the different opium and narcotic acts that have been passed by
Supply-Health

this parliament. Therefore in that consolidation the little oversight to which he refers "'ill undoubtedly be remedied.

Last year prpvision was made in the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act whereby the deportation should be earned out, under certain circumstances, of orientals found guilty of infringing the law. Can the minister tell us how many deportations of orientals have been effected?
Mr. BE I, AND: In complying with ray hon. friend's request for information on one particular feature of the operation of the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act, I might give to the committee some details as to the number of prosecutions which have been carried out by the department. During the ten months of the present fiscal year, ended :51st January, 1923, the total number of prosecutions was as follows:
British Columbia, not including Vancouver; five illicit dealers other than Chinamen, 145 chinamen. Vancouver: eight other than Chinamen; 14 Chinamen.
Alberta: two doctors; 3 dealers other than Chinamen; 26 Chinamen.
Saskatchewan: one dealer other than Chinamen; 10 Chinamen.
Manitoba: two druggists; 16 dealers other than Chinamen; 6 Chinamen.
Ontario, not including Toronto: one veterinary surgeon; 9 dealers other than Chinamen; 52 Chinamen. Toronto: one druggist; 9 dealers other than Chinamen; 37 Chinamen.
Quebec, not including Montreal: one druggist: 21 dealers other than Chinamen; 4 Chinamen. Montreal: ten.doctors; 7 druggists; 55 dealers other than Chinamen ; 124 Chinamen.
New Brunswick: one doctor; 2 dealers, no Chinamen. Nova Scotia: thirteen Chinamen; no others.
Prince Edward Island: none.
This gives a total of 13 doctors, 11 druggists, 1 veterinary surgeon, 129 dealers other than Chinamen, 431 Chinamen, or a grand total of 585 convictions.
How many of the Chinamen were deported?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I am informed that about 30 Chinamen have been deported, and that 200 are awaiting deportation.
I have also a mass of information in connection with the seizure of opium lamps and pipes, decks of opium and other drugs like cocaine, morphine, heroin, and so on/ I do not suppose it is of any interest to the committee to have all those details.
The importation and exportation of narcotic drugs are under license. During the ten months referred to we have issued 161 import licenses, 38 export licenses, 108 wholesale druggist licenses, and 5o retail druggist licenses to manufacturers.

I also have here a table the details of which, sad as it is, should be given to the committee. The table gives a survey of the Dominion and an estimate of the number of addicts in Canada at the present time. It is claimed that there are in British Columbia 2,250 addicts; in Alberta, 350; in Saskatchewan, 250; in Manitoba, 500; in Ontario, 1,800; in Quebec, 3,800; in New Brunswick, 250; in Nova Scotia, 300; and in Prince Edward Island, none. These figures give a total of 9,500.
Would the minister kindly state upon what this estimate is based so that we may have some idea of the authority for it?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: It is based on reports which are constantly coming into the department, mainly from the officials of the Royal Mounted Police. We also secure information from the various religious bodies, from the charitable organizations, from the municipal councils, and different people who take great interest in the operation of this act.

May I also ask the minister if any further steps have been taken to bring about closer co-operation, under the International Conference, towards the suppression of the export of narcotic drugs from other countries? I am not speaking of exportation from Canada, because we do not produce the drugs here, but from Germany, France, where a good deal is manufactured, India, and other countries where it largely originates.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Yes, we are in contact with the League of Nations in this connection. Not very long ago the deputy minister of the department was in Washington in conference with the authorities over there. There is a very heavy traffic, it is assumed, of narcotics, between the United States and Canada. At times it has been supposed that New York was the distributing centre in North America, but it is not an easy task to discover where the distributing centre is. The opinion is now more or less prevalent that Montreal would be the distributing centre. Narcotic drugs are imported clandestinely into Canada by all possible human and inhuman devices. The regular traffic of course, is under control and closely checked. I could tell the House the amount of cocaine and the amount of morphine which has been imported into Canada and also exported, but that amount has been considerably reduced in the last five or six years. The clandestine importation has been on the increase, and it is exceedingly difficult to control. All I can say is that I am not

Supply-Health
thoroughly conversant with all the devices that are being resorted to, in order to unearth the illicit traffickers and dealers. The matter is principally in the hands of the Mounted Police in every large city, especially in Montreal and Vancouver. We have secured a large number of convictions and collected -a certain amount in fines. We have secured penalties to the extent of over $200,000, of which we have been able to collect only $15,000. We are deporting Chinamen as fast as we can. We are making very strenuous efforts to check this very undesirable traffic.

In the case of drug addicts, many of whom are young girls innocently led into the habit, could the minister tell me what efforts are put forth to effect a cure of these victims? Is any systematic effort put forth by the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: My hon. friend will realize that this matter is principally in the hands of the provincial authorities through their social charitable institutions, and in some cases mental institutions. I must confess that the federal Department of Health has not put forth very great effort in this direction because we realize that it does not come principally under our jurisdiction.

I notice further on in the estimates that there is a considerable grant given to the provinces in connection with venereal diseases, the Dominion authorities working in conjunction with the provinces. Would it not be a good step for the Dominion authorities to work in conjunction with the provinces in this matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Yes, there is such an item for the prevention of venereal diseases, but the subject we are dealing with at the present time is entirely different. I do not say that it would not be proper policy to enter into an agreement with the provinces in this regard, but social work is in the hands of municipalities and provinces.

I am very pleased to hear the statement made by the minister, and I desire to say that my experience with his officials and the department having this matter in charge would indicate that every effort is being made to curb this frightful traffic. There is one thought I would like to bring forward just now and it is this: My observation and study of this problem leads me to the conclusion that the energy of those administering the law, both provinciallv and from a federal standpoint, should be concentrated more to destroying the central distributing ring to which he has referred. It is of very little effect to secure a conviction against
an ordinary distributor, or, as we term him, drug peddler, and it is rather strange that after some years of effort I cannot recall any very prominent trafficker being convicted, or even prosecuted. I think the Department of Justice controls our Mounted Police, and if the minister would give instructions to his department, and the ministers would give instructions to the other departments, that the federal officers should be requested to co-operate with the provincial or local officers in a definite manner, with the idea of discovering the central distributing ring, good results might be obtained. There is no question that in Vancouver and Montreal very strong groups exist. It is rumoured that - sometimes fairly prominent citizens may be involved. It matters not to me how prominent a citizen may be, if he is in any way involved in this nefarious traffic, he should not only be exposed,, but the utmost limit of the law, including the lash, should be administered. There have been somewhat strained relations between the different police authorities, such as the Mounted Police, the local police and the provincial police. I know in my province that is the case. Not necessarily strained, but, shall I say, there is a lack in cordial cooperation. This matter is too serious to allow any petty red tape to interfere with the most vigorous administration. I should like to bring that to the attention of the minister. Apropos of that, I notice in the paper to-day the report of a speech delivered by the Attorney General of British Columbia before the Anti-Narcotic Drug League just recently formed, I believe, on the Pacific coast, in which he states that he had been in communication with the minister, and some definite plans had been arrived at to deal with this traffic. Perhaps the minister could inform the committee just what steps had been taken between himself and the Attorney General of British Columbia in this regard.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Since I have been at the bead of the department, our efforts have never been abated for one moment in the effort to secure a closer co-operation between the municipal, provincial and our own police, in the work of suppressing illicit traffic in drugs. Whether we have achieved anything or not I might hesitate to say. I may say frankly that there is a good deal of rivalry between the provincial, the municipal and the Royal Northwest Mounted Police. Each of those worthy bodies claim that they have special immunity of their own, which they will not allow any others to infringe; but if it were possible, as my hon. friend has suggested, to effect that co-operation, our work
Supply-Health

would be more efficient and greatly increased. We have in some respects, though, made some progress in this connection. As regards the co-operation of the national league for the suppression of the traffic, I have also heard a rumour that there was such a league in process of formation, but it is in the infant stage, I am sure. I have no information, whatever, on that score. If it is a worthy association, composed of men of responsible character and standard, we shall be willing, of course, to avail ourselves of its service and co-operation.

I think the minister did not quite catch my last question, which was in regard' to the public statement of the attorney general before this league in Vancouver, when he intimated that something of a definite character had been brought about between himself and the minister by recent correspondence. I was wondering if the minister could give the committee any information on that point.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Nothing that I am aware of.

The minister stated, a few minutes ago, that it was his intention to consolidate the Drug Act this year. In that jvent, I would suggest that he pay some attention to the wording of those sections of the act dealing with the deportation of those convicted, because, if 1 am not very much mistaken, it was found last year in British Columbia that a number of Chinamen convicted could not be deported on account of the terms under which they had been convicted. It appears that if they were sent to jail, they could be deported; but if they were sentenced to a heavy fine, and in default of payment, jailed, they could not be deported. I think if the minister will look into the matter, he will find that a trivial amendment would remedy the situation. I know a number of those convicted got off on habeas corpus for some reason of that kind.
I would also ask the minister to take into cognizance the necessity for increasing the severity of the penalty. I noticed in the press the other day that in Great Britain they have taken power to give men no less than ten years for trafficking in these drugs.

I understand from the minister that fines to the extent of $200,000 have been imposed, while only $15,000 have been collected. Where a fine is not collected, is the person fined sent to prison instead?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Yes, the term of imprisonment is, of course, extended proportionately,

and it is so stated in the statute. One section will provide for a penalty consisting of so much in money and a term of so many months in prison. In case of failure to pay the penalty in cash, the man is retained longer in jail.

I understand this traffic has been growing from year to year, and that it never was so serious as it is at the present moment. How is it then that the appropriation asked for is $20,765 less this year than last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I am informed that though this traffic has been on the increase during the last few years, lately, during the last eight or ten months, to our great satisfaction, some decrease has been shown. There is, indeed, a decrease in the amount of the item; but it was arranged that a part of the amount, which was formerly paid out by the department as expenses to the Royal Mounted Police, would be paid from now on by the Justice department, under which the police operate.
So that the money is expended from some other quarter.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
No. This is to co-operate with the International Joint Commission in the enforcement of any rules and regulations that tiles'- may make in regard to public health.

Supply-Health [DOT]

We have a serious situation on the border line between New Brunswick and the state of Maine where the St. John river is on the boundary on the upper waters of the river. On the Canadian side of the river and on the lower reaches of the river where it runs through New Brunswick, we are strict with our mill owners as regards putting sawdust and refuse into the water, because the salmon are killed thereby. On the upper reaches of the river, where one side of the river is bounded by the state of Maine, we have no control of the United States sawmills. I should like to know if our representative on the International Joint Commission could not take this matter up and have some agreement made with the United States Authorities that they will compel the sawmill owners in the state of Maine to bum their sawdust or dispose of it in some other way than by putting it into the river. This does not affect the fish in the United States part of the river, because just below where the St. John river becomes the international boundary are the Grand Falls on the river, and no salmon can go up over those falls. Therefore, there are no salmon there. But this sawdust flows down and pollutes the river where it runs through New Brunswick entirely, and is very disastrous to salmon. This has been a very important question with us for years. We have taken the matter up, but so far we have not been able to get any relief. I brought the matter to the attention of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe), and he said that something would be done. The situation is a delicate one, but something should be done in the matter by the United States authorities. I would like our representative on the International Joint Commission to take this matter up, and I hope the minister will bring it to his attention.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I will take the necessary
steps to have this matter brought to the attention of my colleague the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe). I think it is a proper subject for the consideration of the International Joint Commission.

I am aware of what my hon. friend from Victoria and Carleton (Mr. Caldwell) has referred to, and I know that the Department of Marine and Fisheries is taking very good care to fine any of our lumbermen who may be caught throwing sawdust and other mill rubbish into the St. John river where that is the international bound-arv. Complaint has been made to the authorities on many occasions that while fines are
imposed on our Canadian lumbermen their rivals in the state of Maine are left free to pollute the river and so destroy the fish. I hope that the Department of Marine and Fisheries and the Department of Health will look into the matter as soon as possible and take the necessary steps to make our American friends respect the law.

Mr. Chairman, the International Joint Commission is very largely a court, and the hon. minister can easily have this matter looked after by laying a complaint before the commission. I have no doubt he will do bo.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, my long list of decreases is now exhausted, and I have to present an item showing an increase of $15,000. This is accounted for by the natural increase in shipping after the _ war and the additional amount required for defraying the salaries of the physicians, the cost of board and the treatment of distressed mariners. As a matter of fact I think that the $95,000 voted last year will be barely sufficient to cover our expenses up to the 1st of April next, and we may have to look after a trifling deficiency in the supplementaries. All the marine hospitals have been closed with the exception of one at Sydney and another at Lunenburg. Provision is made at contract rates for the treatment of sick mariners at local hospitals, or, where there are none, at boarding houses. The dues collected from ships are more than sufficient to defray the expenses.

There has been some complaint from shipping concerns that the dues are too high. Would the minister therefore state what is the comparison between the dues collected and the amount expended, so that we may be informed on the point? Would the minister also kindly give me figures showing the distribution of these cases in the hospitals at the port of Vancouver, which is one of our leading ports?

Quarantine-salaries and contingencies of organized districts; public health in other districts: Tracadie and D'Arey Island Lazarettos, and Public Works Health Act, 1250,000.
How many lepers are there in the Tracadie lazaretto? Have any new cases arisen during the past year? What is the name of the medical officer, his residence and his salary.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: At the Tracadie lazaretto there are six male lepers and five females. The physician in charge there is Dr. Langis. Only one case developed during the past year; it was brought from Montreal.
